h1: The history of whisky in India
title: The History of Whisky in India | Craft Beer School
desc: How whisky came to India with the British, why most Indian whisky is made from molasses and how Indian single malt grew up.
teaser: India drinks whisky on a scale few countries match. Most of it would not be called whisky in Europe. Here is how that happened.
standfirst: Whisky arrived in India with British soldiers and officials. Two centuries later the country drinks it in enormous volumes, mostly as molasses based blends, while a small band of single malt distillers has earned a name abroad. This is the short version of how it all fits together.
sections: Whisky came to India with the British army

Spirits were made in India long before the British arrived. Arrack, toddy and mahua liquor all have deep local roots. Whisky in the Scottish sense came with the East India Company and later the Raj. Soldiers and officials wanted the drinks they knew from home. Importing every bottle by sea around the Cape was slow and expensive.

So production moved closer to the customers. In the 1820s an Englishman named Edward Dyer set up a brewery at Kasauli in the Himalayan foothills, where the cool air and spring water suited brewing. Distilling followed in the hills over the next decades. The British preferred the hill stations for the same reason a brewer still would: in the plains, summer temperatures above 40 °C make fermentation hard to control without refrigeration.

India grows a great deal of sugarcane. Every sugar mill leaves behind molasses, a thick dark syrup that still holds plenty of fermentable sugar. Ferment it, distil it in a column still and you get a strong, clean neutral spirit at low cost.

That neutral spirit became the base of most Indian whisky. Blenders add a share of malt or grain whisky for character, plus flavouring and caramel colour, then reduce it to bottling strength, commonly 42.8% ABV in India. The result is a whisky that is affordable for millions of drinkers. It is also the reason Indian whisky sits in an odd place internationally: the European Union and the UK define whisky as a spirit made from cereal grains, so molasses based blends cannot be sold as whisky there. Our guide to molasses and grain spirit explains the difference in the glass.
Independence turned it into an Indian industry

After 1947 the trade term became IMFL, Indian Made Foreign Liquor: spirits made in India in the style of imported ones. Whisky, rum, brandy and gin all fall under it, but whisky came to dominate. Import duties on foreign spirits were high, which protected domestic brands and kept imported Scotch a luxury for decades.

Alcohol also became a state matter rather than a national one. Each state sets its own excise duty, licences and sales rules. Gujarat has kept prohibition since it was formed in 1960. Bihar introduced it in 2016. A whisky brand in India is really a set of separate state businesses that happen to share a label.
India became one of the world's biggest whisky markets

By volume, India is one of the largest whisky markets in the world. The drinking culture is distinctive too. Whisky is poured with water or soda, often over ice. It is drunk with food rather than after it. A peg, the Indian measure, is usually 30 or 60 ml.

That habit matters when you taste. A whisky built to be drunk long with soda and spicy food is designed differently from one meant to be sipped neat. Judge it on the job it was made for.
Imported Scotch found its way into Indian blends

As India's economy opened up from the 1990s, more drinkers wanted something above the everyday blend. Producers answered in two ways. Some imported Scotch malt whisky in bulk, shipped in tankers or casks at high strength, then blended and bottled it in India. That is why so many Indian labels say blended with Scotch malts or contain imported Scotch. Others imported Scotch already bottled, which carries a much heavier duty and sits at the top of the shelf.

Both moves pushed the market towards what the trade calls premiumisation: fewer but more expensive bottles. They also taught a generation of Indian drinkers what malt whisky tastes like. When Indian single malts arrived, there was already an audience ready to compare them with Scotch. Our guide to Indian single malt picks up the story from there.
Indian single malt changed the conversation

From the mid 2000s, distillers in Bengaluru and Goa began releasing single malts: whisky made only from malted barley, in pot stills, at one distillery. Many used Indian six-row barley grown in Rajasthan and Punjab. Some of these whiskies won serious praise from international judges.

The Indian climate shaped them. Heat speeds up maturation. A cask in a warm Indian warehouse gives up its vanilla, spice and colour much faster than one in a cool Scottish warehouse. The cost is a larger angels' share, the spirit that evaporates through the wood each year. Indian single malts tend to be bottled younger and taste older than their age suggests.
What to taste to understand the story

The history makes more sense in a glass. Pour three whiskies side by side: a mainstream Indian blend, a blended Scotch and an Indian single malt. Nose each one before adding anything. Then add a few drops of water and nose again.

You will usually find the blend light and sweet with a soft spirit edge. The Scotch shows more cereal and some oak. The single malt is likely the richest, with tropical fruit, toffee and spice that come from fast maturation in heat. Naming what you smell takes practice. So does telling the cask from the grain. That is the skill a structured sensory course builds far faster than tasting alone.

Keep the pours small, drink water between them and never drive afterwards. Three 15 ml samples tell you more than three full pegs.
faqs: Under Indian rules it is whisky. In the EU and UK, whisky must be made from cereal grains, so molasses based Indian blends cannot be sold as whisky there. Indian single malts made from malted barley meet the cereal definition.
Why is most Indian whisky made from molasses?
India produces huge amounts of sugarcane and molasses is a by-product of every sugar mill. It ferments easily and makes cheap neutral spirit, which keeps mainstream whisky affordable.
Why does Indian single malt mature faster?
Heat speeds up the reactions between spirit and oak, so the whisky picks up flavour and colour sooner. The trade-off is that more spirit evaporates from each cask every year.
Indian Made Foreign Liquor. It covers spirits made in India in the style of imported ones, such as whisky, rum, brandy and gin.
